summary: Spring Point Ledge Light: a 1897 caisson tower guarding the Portland Harbor ledge that wrecks made a case for; automated 1960, now kept by a trust.

light.current_optic: LED (USLHS record); 36 W incandescent lamp behind a 300 mm plastic Fresnel lens (Trust history)

lens.where: Removed 1960. The Trust says it was found in a private Michigan museum in 2009; LighthouseFriends dates a lawsuit to recover it to 2016.

structures.note: Cast-iron caisson filled with cement (Trust, LighthouseFriends). The NRHP nomination describes a cast-iron superstructure; LighthouseFriends describes white brick.
About 50,000 tons of granite joining the light to Fort Preble. NRHP nomination says 1952.

access.note: USLHS record: open to the public. The Trust has offered tours since 1999 (LighthouseFriends). Check the Trust for current hours.

facts.agency: Spring Point Ledge Light Trust (owner since 1998); the U.S. Coast Guard keeps the aid-to-navigation function under a memorandum of understanding

events.note: Congress appropriates $20,000 for the light and fog-signal station, with a contract limit of $45,000
September storm shatters two sections of the cylinder during setting; over $5,000 in damage
Tower erected 1896-97 by contractor Thomas Dwyer on a cast-iron caisson
Lit 24 May 1897 by first keeper William A. Lane; fifth-order light
Light dark about three months during the Spanish-American War mine scare; resumed 26 July
Schooner Electric Flash runs into the lighthouse in daylight; one lifeboat destroyed
Station electrified by submarine cable from Fort Preble, 1 May 1934
Granite breakwater to Fort Preble completed (Trust and USLHS say 1951; NRHP says 1952)
Original fifth-order Fresnel lens removed; the Trust says it was found in a Michigan private museum in 2009
Transferred to the Spring Point Ledge Light Trust under the Maine Lights Program; deed ceremony 20 June 1998
Trust opens the tower for tours
Heavily corroded roof plates of the main gallery replaced

wrecks.outcome: Barkentine went ashore on Spring Point ledge at 12 o'clock "last night", according to a Portland dispatch dated 21 March 1876 printed in the Daily Kennebec Journal of 22 March, which said she was probably a total loss. The date is approximate: the night of 20-21 March. LighthouseFriends calls her a 393-ton bark and says the crew stayed aboard until dawn.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Trust and the USLHS record give 1951, and the Trust describes the 50,000-ton breakwater as completed that year. The NRHP nomination of 1987 gives 1952. The story gives both.

notes_for_editor: (0) No woman keeper, or family member who kept the light in her own right, appears in the USLHS roster or in the sources read for this station. Disputed or unverified points, for a human look. (1) Breakwater year: 1951 (Trust, USLHS) against 1952 (NRHP). (2) Superstructure material: NRHP says cast iron; LighthouseFriends says white brick. The story says the sources differ. (3) Original lens: the Trust says it was found in a Michigan private museum in 2009; LighthouseFriends dates a Justice Department lawsuit in Michigan to 2016. Both are cited; neither is checked against a court record. (4) Current optic: USLHS says LED; the Trust's history describes an incandescent lamp behind a 300 mm plastic lens. The Trust page may be out of date. (5) The keeper roster is the USLHS roster, derived from NARA registers per the archive. It was not checked against the NARA registers. Lines are as printed. Joseph Bakken's entry is open (1954-); no personal detail is used. (6) The 1876 wreck date is approximate: the Kennebec Journal says 'last night' in its 22 March issue. (7) The fog bell and Lane/Phillips first-lighting are in the USLHS roster and the Trust; the 1897 Board report shows 24 May 1897 for the light and the bell. (8) Two wreck or harbor incidents rest on LighthouseFriends alone: the crew walking ashore on a plank (1876) and the 1933 keeper quotation (as quoted by LighthouseFriends from an unnamed local paper). (9) Not used: the 1832 Nancy fire and the 1951 Corps of Engineers breakwater authorization in LighthouseFriends, which the story does not need. (10) The NRHP OCR is poor in places ('keeper f s quarters'); evidence quotes avoid the garbled words. (11) The record's '1988 nrhp_listed' date and 'Fl W 6s' characteristic were not verified in any source read for this story. Fact-check pass 2026-10-22: (a) The story now says the Board's first recommendation is disputed: the Trust gives April 1891, the NRHP form says requests began in 1892, and the 1894 report says the request was made in its last three annual reports. (b) Lens dates: both the Trust and LighthouseFriends date the lens's location to 2009; LighthouseFriends dates the Justice Department lawsuit to 2016 and gives no date for the Coast Guard taking possession. The earlier claim that the two accounts gave different dates for the lens's recovery was removed as unsupported. (c) Vessel rig: the Kennebec Journal says barkentine; LighthouseFriends says 393-ton bark. The story gives both. (d) The 1894 report's 'last three annual reports' wording is quoted from the archive text (scan pp. 350-351). (e) Tower visiting: the Trust page gives no hours, so the story cites LighthouseFriends for summer opening and occasional tower access; check the Trust or the Coast Guard before a visit.
